James Ramsay
jāmz ram'zē
n. (James Ramsay, 1733–1789, naval surgeon turned Anglican priest in St Kitts, first insider witness against West Indian slavery)
Scottish surname Ramsay, from a place name, the ram's island or wild-garlic island.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

James Ramsay was a Scottish naval surgeon who in 1759 was ordered aboard a slave ship with an epidemic on it, and never recovered from what he saw between decks. He took orders and served parishes in St Kitts for nineteen years, where he attempted to catechize and baptize the enslaved and was boycotted by his own planter vestries for it. He came home and in 1784 published An Essay on the Treatment and Conversion of African Slaves in the British Sugar Colonies, the first detailed account of the system by a man who had administered sacraments inside it. The planter interest answered with pamphlets attacking his character, and he spent his last five years supplying Wilberforce and the Commons committees with evidence, dying in 1789 in the middle of the fight. Jer 22:13 names the thing he described, the man who “useth his neighbour's service without wages” (Jer 22:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a planter as one who owns a plantation, and testimony as a solemn declaration made for establishing some fact.

expand to see more

PLANT'ER, n. One who plants, sets, introduces or establishes; one who owns a plantation; used in the West Indies and Southern states of America.

TES'TIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.

MEN'STEALER, n. One who steals men; one who kidnaps.

Key Scripture

Jer 22:13 — "Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour's service without wages, and giveth him not for his work;"

1Ti 1:10 — "For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;"

Phm 1:16 — "Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?"

Mat 5:11 — "Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake."

Modern Corruption

Nineteen years inside the system, one book, and five years of being called a liar for writing it.

expand to see more

Ramsay's evidence was decisive because it was not hearsay. He had buried the dead, attempted the catechism, and been obstructed by the men whose interest it was; and he could answer the planters' standard defences from inside. 1Ti 1:10 puts menstealers in the list of the lawless, and Phm 1:16 shows Paul returning a runaway as “a brother beloved” (Phm 1:16), which is the relation the colonial church could not maintain and a slave code cannot allow.

The corruption to name is the use of the parish church as an instrument of the estate. Ramsay's vestries did not object to religion; they objected to a religion administered to the enslaved on the same terms as to themselves, because a sacrament implies a soul and a soul implies a brother. Mat 5:11 is what he received for pressing it, men saying “all manner of evil against you falsely” (Mat 5:11). He died before the trade was touched and the men who carried it had his papers.

Usage

"“useth his neighbour's service without wages” (Jer 22:13) — the system he described."

"“a brother beloved” (Phm 1:16) — the relation a slave code forbids."

"“shall say all manner of evil against you falsely” (Mat 5:11) — his last five years."
